title: Chapter 91: Day and Night 2
content:
Chapter 91

Wei Wuxian went into an absolute picking frenzy, shamelessly stripping the stems until the skiff was practically buried under a mountain of bright green lotus pods. There was barely anywhere left to put their feet, leaving the three of them essentially marooned in a sea of lotus heads. He cracked open the spongy green rinds to reveal rows of tender pods nestled inside fluffy brown pith. Popped from their hulls and peeled clean, the seeds were snowy white, crisp, and bursting with sweet, refreshing juice; even the delicate green sprouts nestled in their cores were sweet, carrying not a trace of bitterness.

Wen Ning stayed parked at the bow, peeling pod after pod with mechanical focus. Lan Wangji ate a pair he had peeled himself and then called it quits; whenever Wen Ning tried to pass over a handful of fresh seeds, Lan Wangji simply shook his head, gesturing for them to go straight to Wei Wuxian. Wei Wuxian single-handedly devoured an entire boatload of them. Drifting with the current for another couple of hours, they finally bumped against the stone docks of Yunping City.

The shallows around the wharf were crowded with small fishing skiffs. A cluster of local women knelt along the stone steps beating laundry, while a flock of sun-bronzed, shirtless boys splashed in and out of the river, diving like otters. The sight of an unfamiliar skiff lazily drifting toward them caught everyone's eye. The guy at the stern had his head tucked low, but the two young men in the middle were absolute knockouts. The man sitting up front was draped in robes as pristine as fresh snow, radiating an otherworldly, untouchable poise; the young man beside him was a grinning, devastatingly handsome charmer. Figures of this caliber were a rare sight in these waters, and the whole bank froze, gawking openly.

A handful of swimming boys darted over like a school of fish, seven or eight wet heads bobbing around the gunwales.

Wei Wuxian flashed an easy grin. "Excuse me, folks—is this Yunping City?"

One of the laundry girls blushed crimson and piped up, "Sure is! This is Yunping!"

"We're here," Wei Wuxian said, stretching. "Let's head up."

As the boat touched the wharf, Lan Wangji was the first to step onto the stone landing, turning back to offer Wei Wuxian a hand. The two stepped onto the dock without a hitch, but Wen Ning was hopelessly trapped on board. Seeing his sickly pale skin, the pitch-black hairline cracks sprawling across his neck and cheeks, and his silent, awkward slouch, the boys in the water weren't scared in the slightest—they found him hilarious. A dozen small hands latched onto the gunwales, rocking the skiff violently back and forth until Wen Ning was swaying just to keep his balance.

Wei Wuxian glanced back over his shoulder. "Hey! What are you kids doing? Leave him alone."

Wen Ning looked up with a helpless grimace. "Gongzi... I can't get off."

Before he could finish his plea, two of the boys slapped the water with their palms, sending a volley of river spray straight into his face. Wen Ning could only wear a bitter, resigned smile. If these kids had any earthly idea that the "guy" they were splashing could tear them limb from limb with his bare hands and grind their bones to dust, they’d have drowned from sheer terror.

Wei Wuxian scooped up the last handful of lotus pods from the deck and hurled them over their heads. "Fetch!"

The boys broke apart instantly, scrambling over one another to chase the treats. Taking advantage of the clear water, Wen Ning awkwardly hopped ashore, giving the soaked hem of his robes a sheepish shake.

Yunping was easily one of the more prosperous hubs in the Yunmeng region—sprawling, lively, and bustling with activity. The trio stepped past the city gates into streets packed with foot traffic and dazzling storefronts. Wen Ning had never been a fan of crowds, and within a few paces, he silently slipped into the background and vanished.

Wei Wuxian followed the street names he remembered from the deed, asking for directions along the way. But when they finally arrived at the location and took a good look at the building before them, both he and Lan Wangji froze.

Staring up at the grand, imposing entrance, bathed in thick clouds of incense smoke and bustling with pilgrims, Wei Wuxian blinked. "This is... a Guanyin Temple?"

Lan Wangji murmured, "Mm."

Jin Guangyao was the last person on earth anyone would mistake for a pious devotee. The two traded an unreadable glance, then stepped past the steady stream of pilgrims and over the high wooden threshold. It was a traditional three-hall complex, the air heavy with swirling incense and the steady, rhythmictock-tockof wooden fish. It didn't take long to circle the grounds.

Their final stop was the main sanctuary housing the grand statue of Guanyin. They hadn't lingered by the entrance for more than a breath before a monk approached with palms pressed together, bowing in greeting. The two returned the salute.

After trading polite pleasantries, Wei Wuxian casually remarked, "Temples are usually tucked away deep in the mountains. It's quite rare to find one planted right in the heart of a bustling city."

The monk offered a warm smile. "Those living in the city spend their days chasing livelihoods and toiling away. Do they not have an even greater need for a sanctuary like this to pray, make wishes, and seek inner peace?"

Wei Wuxian chuckled softly. "Doesn't the hustle and bustle disturb the Bodhisattva's peace?"

"The Bodhisattva delivers all sentient beings from suffering," the monk replied serenely. "How could she ever be disturbed by the mortal world?"

"Is this temple dedicated solely to Guanyin?"

"Indeed."

After making a couple more rounds through the courtyards to take mental notes, they stepped out into the streets. Wei Wuxian pulled Lan Wangji into a quiet, shadowed alley, grabbed a stray twig from the dirt, and sketched out a rough layout of the grounds.

Tossing the branch aside, he muttered, "Jin Guangyao really spared no expense."

Lan Wangji picked the twig back up, adding several clean strokes over the squares. The blueprint snapped into sharp focus, forming a precise bird's-eye map of the temple they had just left.

Wei Wuxian took the branch back from his fingers, tapping the center. "There’s a massive suppression array woven into the temple grounds. Something is pinned beneath it." He tapped a specific focal point. "The layout is intricate and airtight, but crack this array eye, and whatever is locked down there is coming out."

Lan Wangji straightened up. "We break the array tonight, once the crowds have cleared. For now, we find lodgings to rest and consolidate our plans."

With no idea how volatile the suppressed creature might be, pulling the pin during the day with hundreds of pilgrims around was out of the question.

Wei Wuxian mused, "Any idea how long cleaning up whatever's in there will take? Will we still make it to Lanling in time, or will this throw off our schedule?"

Lan Wangji looked at him, his gaze steady. "Your condition is still unstable. Do not push yourself."

The battle at the Burial Mounds had completely drained Wei Wuxian, keeping his mind and nerves stretched to the absolute breaking point. Barely a few hours ago, Jiang Cheng’s vitriol had pushed him to the verge of coughing up a lungful of blood, and he was only just regaining his footing. Even if he felt fine right now, dragging a secretly battered body into Lanling on sheer stubbornness was asking for an unexpected collapse at a critical moment.

Besides, he wasn't the only one running on fumes—Lan Wangji hadn't had a wink of real rest over the last two days either. Even if Wei Wuxian could afford to be reckless, Lan Wangji needed to catch his breath.

Wei Wuxian relented. "Alright. Let's find a place to crash first."

On his own, Wei Wuxian could sleep anywhere—feather beds if he had the coin, tree roots if he was broke. But with Lan Wangji at his side, the mere thought of making Hanguang-jun curl up in the dirt or cram into some flea-bitten hovel was entirely off the table.

After combing the streets, they settled on a respectable, high-end inn on the far side of town. The proprietress practically lunged out the front door, beaming as she ushered them inside. The tavern was spotless, bustling with patrons on the ground floor—a clear sign of a sharp, capable manager. Nearly all the staff were women, ranging from fresh-faced teenage girls sweeping the floors to broad-shouldered aunties manning the stoves.

The moment the two men crossed the threshold, eyes lit up across the room. One young maid pouring water was staring so hard at Lan Wangji that the kettle’s spout completely missed the cup, spilling hot tea over the table without her even noticing. The landlady barked a quick reprimand to snap her staff back to work, then personally escorted the two upstairs to inspect the rooms.

"How many rooms will the young masters be needing?" she asked over her shoulder.

The casual question made Wei Wuxian’s heart do an immediate, violent flip. He cast a careful, sideways glance at Lan Wangji.

Two months ago, this wouldn't have even been a question. Back when he first returned in Mo Xuanyu's body, he had pulled out every shameless, degenerate trick in the book to repulse Lan Wangji and get kicked out of the Cloud Recesses. Lan Wangji had caught onto the game immediately, which was why he began booking only a single room wherever they went—knowing full well that no matter how many rooms they had, Wei Wuxian would inevitably crawl into his bed anyway.

And with his true identity concealed, Wei Wuxian had known no shame. On their very first night descending from Gusu, he hadn't even waited for Lan Wangji to wash up before shamelessly burrowing into his covers. When Lan Wangji pushed the door open to find him rolling around on the mattress, he’d stood expressionless for a moment before turning on his heel to sleep in the second room he’d booked next door. But Wei Wuxian was relentless; he’d chased him right into the adjoining room, throwing a tantrum about sleeping together. Once he scrambled onto the mattress, he’d chucked Lan Wangji’s spare pillow out the open window, insisting they share one, and loudly interrogated Lan Wangji on why he was sleeping in his robes, hands flying to strip him down by force. In the dead of night, he’d shoved his freezing feet straight under Lan Wangji’s blanket, clamping Lan Wangji’s hand over his own chest with wide, teary eyes—"Feel how fast my heart is beating, Hanguang-jun!"—only to be struck with a swift, paralyzing tap that left him frozen like a board until morning.

Looking back on those stunts now, Wei Wuxian felt a cold sweat break out. For the first time in his two lives, he was genuinely appalled by his own sheer shamelessness.

Stealing a third glance, he found Lan Wangji looking down, face completely unreadable.

With the silence dragging on, Wei Wuxian’s thoughts began to spiral:Lan Zhan always asks for one room. Why isn't he speaking up today? If he asks for two rooms this time, it means he really took Jiang Cheng's words to heart and wants to draw a line. But even if he asks for one room, that doesn't mean he's fine with it—maybe he's just keeping up appearances so I don't feel awkward...

While he was busy tying his brain into knots, the landlady took matters into her own hands. With brisk, cheerful certainty, she declared, "One room it is! One room will do nicely! Our suites have plenty of space for two. The bed won't be cramped at all."

Lan Wangji didn't object.

Only then did Wei Wuxian’s feet feel like they were touching solid ground again, his racing pulse settling back down.

The landlady pushed open a heavy wooden door, gesturing them inside. The suite was indeed spacious. "Will the young masters be taking dinner? Our cook has incredible hands—I can have a spread sent right up once it's ready?"

Wei Wuxian nodded. "Yes, please. Not right now, though. Later in the evening—have it brought up around eight."

"Right away, young master!" the landlady beamed, turning to leave.

She had barely cleared the threshold when Wei Wuxian abruptly caught the door, slipping out into the corridor. "Ma'am!"

She paused. "Something else I can get you, sir?"

As if bracing himself for an ordeal, Wei Wuxian lowered his voice. "When you send dinner up tonight... bring along some liquor. The stronger, the better."

The landlady grinned knowingly. "Say no more!"

With the order placed, he casually stepped back inside, shut the door, and took a seat at the table.

Lan Wangji immediately reached across, pressing two fingers over his pulse. Wei Wuxian knew full well this was just a standard medical check, but as those cool, slender fingers slid along his wrist, lightly working their way up his forearm, the fingers of his free hand curled into a tight, quiet fist beneath the table.

After half an hour of meticulous examination, Lan Wangji drew his hand back. "You are fine."

Wei Wuxian stretched his arms with an easy chuckle. "Thanks." Catching the severe furrow lingering between Lan Wangji’s brows, he softened his tone. "Hanguang-jun, are you worried about Ze-wu-jun? I suspect Jin Guangyao still holds a sliver of genuine respect for your brother. Besides, Ze-wu-jun outmatches him in raw cultivation and is already on guard; he won't be taken down easily. We’ll crack this temple array tonight and try to hit the road again by tomorrow."

Lan Wangji murmured, "This matter is strange."

Wei Wuxian blinked. "How so?"

"My brother and Jin Guangyao have been close for years," Lan Wangji said. "Jin Guangyao is not an impulsive man driven by bloodlust. He does not strike blindly."

"Mm. That matches my impression of him too," Wei Wuxian agreed. "Jin Guangyao isn't soft by any stretch, but he goes out of his way to avoid making unnecessary enemies."

Lan Wangji looked up. "What transpired at the Burial Mounds was reckless, grand, and rushed. It does not fit his nature."

Wei Wuxian considered it. "True. If his gambit on the mountain succeeded, he’d wipe the slate clean. But the moment it fell apart, he effectively forced every single sect in the realm into open war against him. The risk was astronomical."

Lan Wangji’s voice was quiet, heavy with thought. "There may be deeper layers yet to uncover."
